newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Minghella dedicated to English Patient's survival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Minghella dedicated to English Patient's survival.

text.p: Anthony Minghella had no idea what he was getting himself into when he picked up a copy of Michael Ondaatje's novel "The English Patient".
He was so enthralled that he read the book in "one gulp" and decided he would try to turn the novel into a screenplay.

That turned out to be the easy part. Making a film of the screenplay was a grinding, often dispiriting, slog that has, however, transformed his career and put him in line for a best director's Oscar at the Academy Awards ceremony next Monday.
"It's made out of love for the book," he said of the film. "I was trying to be the best reader I could."

Set in Egypt and Tuscany during World War Two, "The English Patient" pulls together passion, adventure and the tragedy of war to tell a heart-wrenching story of four damaged people, thrown together by chance.

Minghella's initial challenge was to figure out a way of telling a story which constantly switches between two different times in separate countries with only one character holding the narrative together.
Born to Italian parents and brought up on England's Isle of Wight, 43-year-old Minghella confesses to knowing little about 1940s Italy and even less about Egypt.

His solution reflected his background as an academic. He borrowed a cottage in the heart of the English countryside and buried himself in books about military history and diaries of soldiers in North Africa and southern Italy.
Minghella said his Italian roots and British upbringing gave him an ability to understand what it was to be English but at the same time maintain an outsider's perspective.
"It's a very useful thing, it's not a problem. It gives you a view," he said in a lecture organised by the Guardian newspaper.
MINGHELLA CONVINCED FILM WOULD BE SUCCESS
The film's original financiers, 20th Century Fox, pulled out of the project just before shooting was due to begin, leaving Minghella having to convince Miramax Films that he could make them a profit.
"I went into every meeting with a sign flashing over my head saying 'his films don't make any money'", he joked.

But along with Ondaatje and the film's producer, Saul Zaentz, Minghella was convinced he could make a success of "The English Patient". "All three of us felt that if we made the film with passion, adults would watch," he said.

Minghella's previous films were low-budget productions -- "Truly, Madly Deeply", a huge success in Britain, and "Mr. Wonderful". He spent much of his career working in the theatre and this honed his ability to get the best out of a cast.
"I think the thing I learnt in the theatre was to rely on actors," he said.
His insistence on Kristin Scott Thomas, and not a better known Hollywood star, playing the leading female role was crucial to his vision of the film coming to fruition.

He also felt Ralph Fiennes was the ideal actor to play Count Almasy, the central character. "He called and said he wanted to do the film and it took me about 1/4 of a second to say 'yes'", Minghella said. Both actors are also in line for Oscars.
DESERT PRESENTED BIGGEST PROBLEM
Once the casting was in place, he then had to tackle his biggest problem -- the desert.
Mistakes could not be made shooting scenes in sand dunes as the footprints took days to disappear. "In the first week I was there I felt like I was going mad," Minghella said.
The film crew spent 123 days on location, battling with freezing weather at night and a scorching sun during the day. It took Minghella a further 10-1/2 months to complete the film.

"I was extremely nervous of this film and extremely nervous of what we had achieved," he said. "I tried to get anybody I knew to come and look at the film. I wanted to make sure I had done everything I could before I abandoned it."
The burden of making such a complex and demanding film has prevented him from returning to his home and family for all but a few days over the past two years.
The hard grind may be worth it as "The English Patient" has been nominated for 12 Oscars, setting a new British record by surpassing the 11 received by Richard Attenborough's "Gandhi".
But now that he has put "The English Patient" to bed, his intentions are clear.
"It's taken so long, we've been in this tunnel so long that I just can't wait to be a human being again. That's my project."
